question: Under SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5: what maximum security strength can SHA-1 provide when used for digital signatures and when used for HMAC, and may it still be used to generate digital signatures on federal information? What assumptions sit behind the HMAC, KMAC, key-derivation and random-bit-generation column of the hash-strength table? Which hash functions are the smallest that give 128-bit strength for digital signatures? And what strength results (a) when a 256-bit key generated by a 256-bit RBG and used with AES-256 is wrapped with AES-128, and (b) when a 224-bit ECC key is used under SP 800-56A to establish a 128-bit AES key?

facets.text: For digital signatures (collision resistance) SHA-1 is rated at <= 80 bits - it has been shown to give less than 80 bits - so it is no longer approved for generating signatures on federal information, though verifying already-protected information may be allowed if the risk is accepted.

evidence.quote: SHA-1 has been demonstrated to provide less than 80 bits of security for digital signatures, which require collision resistance

hash functions and applications providing less than 112 bits of security strength ( i.e., ≤ 80, as shown in orange above) are no longer approved for applying cryptographic protection for federal government information

facets.text: For HMAC (and KDFs and random bit generation) SHA-1 is listed at 128 bits; the HMAC rating assumes pre-image rather than collision resistance (footnote 70).

evidence.quote: Assumes that pre-image resistance is required rather than collision resistance

facets.text: Assumptions: HMAC/KMAC keys with length and entropy at least equal to the security strength; key derivation assumes the shared secret or key has sufficient entropy; random bit generation assumes adequate entropy. (The table also notes that KMAC is based on a FIPS 202 function rather than an approved hash function; not required.)

evidence.quote: the estimated security strength assumes that the length and entropy used to generate the key are at least equal to the security strength
The security strength for key-derivation assumes that the shared secret or key used contains sufficient entropy to support the desired security strength
The security strength for random bit generation assumes that the random bit generator has been provided with adequate entropy
KMAC is not technically based on an approved hash function but is based on a function specified in FIPS 202

facets.text: Smallest for 128-bit signature strength: SHA-256, SHA-512/256 and SHA3-256 (larger ones such as SHA-512 may also be used).

evidence.quote: a security strength of 128 bits can be provided using SHA-512

facets.text: (a) Wrapping with AES-128 reduces the key's strength to 128 bits even though it is still used with AES-256.

evidence.quote: However, if the key is wrapped using AES
is reduced to 128 bits even though it is still used with AES256

facets.text: (b) No more than 112 bits, because a 224-bit ECC key provides at most 112 bits.

evidence.quote: if a 224-bit ECC key is used as specified in SP 800-56A to establish a 128bit AES key, no more than 112 bits of security can be provided

reference_answer: Table 3 rates SHA-1 at <= 80 bits for digital signatures (it has been shown to give less than 80 bits of collision resistance), so it is no longer approved for applying protection such as generating signatures on federal information, although processing already-protected data may be allowed if the risk is accepted. SHA-1 is listed at 128 bits in the HMAC/KMAC/KDF/RBG column; for HMAC this assumes pre-image rather than collision resistance (footnote 70). That column assumes HMAC/KMAC keys whose length and entropy at least match the strength, KDF secrets and RBGs with sufficient entropy, and notes KMAC is built on a FIPS 202 function rather than an approved hash. The smallest hash functions for 128-bit signature strength are SHA-256, SHA-512/256 and SHA3-256 (larger ones such as SHA-512 also qualify). (a) Wrapping the AES-256 key with AES-128 cuts its strength to 128 bits; (b) a 224-bit ECC key limits the established AES key to 112 bits.
notes: Table 3 and its footnotes 70-74 (PDF p.69, printed 56); approval note p.70 (printed 57); combination examples in 5.6.2 (pp.70-71, printed 57-58). Trap: SHA-1's two different ratings (<= 80 vs 128) depend on the application. Table 2 key sizes and Table 4 time frames are not needed; RSA-2048 is covered by H's earlier dev question h_nist57_002 (dev.jsonl).

checks.author: Read pp.67-72.
checks.verifier: Blind answer matched f1-f6; the comparison found the key over-reached on footnote 70 and on HMAC use - fixed as noted below. Red-team review: fix applied: footnote 70 tied to HMAC only; f3 lists the HMAC/KMAC, KDF and RBG assumptions and makes the KMAC FIPS 202 note non-required; question asks only about generating digital signatures.

question: According to Apple's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, how many iPhone units did Apple sell in fiscal 2025, and what was the iPhone's average selling price?

The 'stand-alone selling prices (SSPs)' on p.38 are a revenue-allocation method with no figures, not an average selling price. question: Under SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, which kinds of key information must receive confidentiality protection, which must receive integrity protection, and which must receive availability protection? According to Table 5, what security protection, association protection, assurances and period of protection apply to (a) a private signature key, (b) a public signature-verification key and (c) a symmetric authentication key? What must happen to symmetric and private keys at the end of their period of protection, and how can the period of protection for integrity differ from that for confidentiality?

facets.text: Confidentiality protection is required for all secret key information (symmetric keys, private keys, key shares, secret metadata); public keys, domain parameters and most metadata generally do not need it.

evidence.quote: onfidentiality protection shall be provided for all secret key information
Public keys, domain parameters, and much of the metadata generally do not require confidentiality protection

facets.text: Integrity protection is required for all key information; availability protection for all key information needed beyond its immediate use (via backup or archiving).

evidence.quote: Integrity protection shall be provided for all key information
Availability protection shall be provided for all key information that needs to be available beyond its immediate use

facets.text: (a) Private signature key: confidentiality and integrity; associations with usage or application, domain parameters (when used) and the public signature-verification key; assurance of possession; protected from generation until the end of the cryptoperiod.

evidence.quote: Private signature key | Source authentication Integrity authentication Support for non-repudiation | Confidentiality Integrity 80 | Usage or application Domain parameters (when used) Public signature- verification key | Possession | From generation until the end of the cryptoperiod

facets.text: (b) Public signature-verification key: integrity and availability; associations with usage or application, key pair owner, domain parameters (when used), the private signature key and signed data; assurance of validity; protected from generation until no protected data needs to be verified.

evidence.quote: Public signature- verification key | Source authentication Integrity authentication Support for non-repudiation | Integrity Availability | Usage or application Key pair owner Domain parameters (when used) Private signature key Signed data | Validity | From generation until no protected data needs to be verified

facets.text: (c) Symmetric authentication key: confidentiality, integrity and availability; associations with usage or application, other authorized entities and authenticated data; no assurance listed; protected from generation until no protected data needs to be verified.

evidence.quote: Symmetric authentication key | Identity authentication Integrity authentication | Confidentiality Integrity Availability | Usage or application Other authorized entities Authenticated data |  | From generation until no protected data needs to be verified

facets.text: Symmetric and private keys shall be destroyed at the end of their period of protection; integrity protection may only be needed until a key is no longer used, whereas confidentiality protection may be needed until the key is actually destroyed.

evidence.quote: Symmetric keys and private keys shall be destroyed at the end of their period of protection
Integrity protection may only be required until a key is no longer used (but not yet destroyed), but confidentiality protection may be required until the key is actually destroyed

reference_answer: Confidentiality protection is required for all secret key information - symmetric keys, private keys, key shares and secret metadata - but generally not for public keys, domain parameters or most metadata. Integrity protection is required for all key information, and availability protection for all key information needed beyond its immediate use (provided by backup or archiving). Table 5: (a) a private signature key needs confidentiality and integrity, association with its usage/application, domain parameters (when used) and the public verification key, assurance of possession, and protection from generation to the end of the cryptoperiod; (b) a public signature-verification key needs integrity and availability, association with usage/application, the key pair owner, domain parameters, the private key and the signed data, assurance of validity, and protection until no protected data needs to be verified; (c) a symmetric authentication key needs confidentiality, integrity and availability, association with usage/application, other authorized entities and the authenticated data, no listed assurance, and protection until no protected data needs to be verified. Symmetric and private keys shall be destroyed at the end of their period of protection; integrity protection may end when a key is no longer used, while confidentiality may be needed until the key is destroyed.
notes: Section 6.1 (PDF pp.78-79, printed 65-66) and Table 5's first rows with the 'Guide to Table 5' (p.80, printed 67). Docling drops the drop-cap 'C' ('C onfidentiality'). Table 5 continues over several pages; only the three rows on p.80 are asked. Footnote 80 on integrity means is not asked.
